<result># Research report: making the web agent faster and cheaper without losing accuracy

I checked your `codex/subminute-runtime` branch before writing this. `docs/12-optimization-analysis.md` puts the current version (C) at about 300–430 s and about $0.10 per run. That splits into roughly 157 navigation calls (about 62% of cost), and uncached navigation input alone is about 50% of cost. The docs estimate about 2.5x more navigation decisions than needed, mostly from 18–22 `wait_for` polling calls per run and from separate "extract" and "navigate" steps. The analysis is consistent across sources: **the main lever is fewer navigation decisions, not cheaper tokens.** The recommendations below are ranked with that in mind.

Labels: [P] peer-reviewed paper, [V] vendor-reported, [I] my inference.

---

## 1. Observation compression

| Technique | Mechanism | Reported gain | Fit for us | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **AgentOccam observation simplification** [P, ICLR'25] | Merges static text into the interactive node with the same label. Turns tables and lists into Markdown. Replays only "pivotal nodes" from history (nodes the model names, plus their ancestors, siblings and children). Drops steps from abandoned plan branches. | On a 190-task dev split with GPT-4-Turbo, cumulative success went 14.2 → 25.8 (fewer actions) → 30.0 (no scrolling, full page) → 34.7 (simplified observation) → 36.8 (pivotal history) → 44.2 (planning). **Tokens per step went up** (2210 → 2931) because the whole page is loaded. Steps per task 6.2 → 9.0. | High, and cheap to build. Markdown tables matter a lot for the ERP stock and price-condition grids. Pivotal-node history replaces raw step logs. | https://arxiv.org/html/2410.13825 |
| **Agent-E DOM distillation** [P] | The agent picks one of three DOM views per call: `text_only` (inner text), `input_fields` (compact JSON of interactive elements), `all_fields`. | 73.2% on WebVoyager. No per-mode token numbers. | High. Make the observation mode a tool argument: `input_fields` for forms and the configurator, `text_only` for spec documents and mails. Removes about 14k characters of irrelevant content from many steps [I]. | https://arxiv.org/html/2407.13032v1 |
| **Prune4Web** [P, AAAI'26] | The LLM writes only a `keyword_weights` dict (weights 1–50). A fixed Python template (rapidfuzz plus a stemmer) scores elements by tier (visible text > aria-label/placeholder > class/id) and match type (exact > phrase > word > fuzzy). The top 20 go to the grounder. | 25–50x fewer candidates. Zero-shot GPT-4o-mini filter: Recall@20 89%, grounding 67.6 → 73.8%. Zero-shot GPT-4o Recall@3 is only about 72%. | Medium-high. About 100 lines of Python. Only useful on large pages; our internal sites are probably small. | https://arxiv.org/html/2511.21398 |
| **Mind2Web / MindAct ranking** [P] | A DeBERTa cross-encoder ranks elements and the LLM chooses from the top-k. | A third-party ranker card reports recall@10 of about 93%. | Low. Needs a GPU model and training data, and is overkill for our sites. | https://huggingface.co/torontodeveloper/mind2web-candidate-ranker |
| **WebLINX Dense Markup Ranker** [P] | A dual encoder embeds turn state and elements separately, then ranks by cosine similarity. Cheaper than a cross-encoder. | No isolated recall figure. | Low-medium. BM25 over element text plus attributes gets most of the benefit at no cost [I]. | https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.05930 |
| **D2Snap** [P, 2025] | Downsamples the DOM by merging and averaging subtrees, analogous to JPEG compression, and keeps hierarchy. | 67% vs 65% for a screenshot baseline on Online-Mind2Web at the same token scale. Finding: hierarchy matters. | Medium. Open source (github.com/surfly/D2Snap). Main lesson: keep indentation and hierarchy, don't flatten. | https://arxiv.org/html/2508.04412v2 |
| **LCoW** [P, ICLR'25] | A separate contextualizer LM rewrites the page into a task-relevant summary before the actor sees it. | +15.6 points (closed models) and +23.7 points (open models) on WorkArena. | Adds an LLM call per step, the opposite of our goal. Only helps if the contextualizer replaces several actor steps. | https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.10689 |
| **"Read More, Think More"** [P, 2026] | Systematic study of observation reduction. | Compact AX trees help weaker models; full HTML helps stronger or thinking models; long inputs make weak models hallucinate; **diff-based history is the token-efficient way to keep history.** | Qwen-Flash with no thinking is the "weaker model" case here, so reduce. Use diffs: "page unchanged except X". | https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01535 |
| **AutoWebGLM, Dripper, SCRIBES** [P] | Rule-based HTML pruning (drop script, style, nav, footer; whitelist attributes). SCRIBES deduplicates repeated siblings. | SCRIBES: about 114k → 17k tokens (-85%) from sibling deduplication. | High for the webmail and Q&A lists: collapse N similar rows to a template plus values, or paginate in code. | https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.01832 |

**Diff observations [I, backed by the 2604.01535 guideline]:** hash each text block. After an action, send only added or changed blocks plus a one-line summary of the rest. This cuts tokens on the many steps where only a dropdown's options change, which is typical of cascading selects.

## 2. Fewer LLM calls (the main lever)

- **Multi-action per step (browser-use `max_actions_per_step`)** [V]: the model outputs a list of actions. The runtime executes them in order and **stops the batch as soon as the page or DOM changes**, then re-observes. That stop rule is what makes batching safe. Your `steps` tool already does this for forms and cut submission from about 51–57 calls to 27. Extend it to navigation, e.g. "open these 5 mail rows, extract each" as one call. https://docs.browser-use.com/customize/agent/all-parameters
- **browser-use `flash_mode`** [V]: "skips evaluation, next goal and thinking and only uses memory." Output shrinks to roughly memory plus action. Their speed post measured output tokens at about 215x the per-token latency of input tokens (1k input = 29 ms; 10 output = 63 ms). They also put **history before the fresh browser state so the prefix stays KV-cacheable**, and keep action names terse (10–15 output tokens). They report about 3 s per step and 68 s per task on Online-Mind2Web for BU 1.0 [V, self-hosted benchmark]. https://browser-use.com/posts/speed-matters
- **Plan-and-Act** [P, ICML'25]: a planner writes high-level steps and an executor grounds them, with replanning after each executor phase. 57.6% on WebArena-Lite, but the gain comes from a fine-tuned planner on synthetic data. A day-sized version: one planner call per site emits a checklist (you already have code checklists), and the executor runs a batch per item. https://arxiv.org/html/2503.09572v3
- **LLMCompiler** [P, ICML'24]: the planner emits a DAG of tool calls and the executor runs independent nodes in parallel. Up to 3.7x lower latency and 6.7x lower cost vs ReAct (best-case, on QA tool tasks, not web). Applies to fan-out: "open these 18 mails / these 6 Q&A pages / these N ERP materials" in parallel tabs from one decision. https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.04511
- **ReWOO** [P, 2023]: plan once with variable placeholders and execute without intermediate observations. The paper reports about 5x token efficiency on HotpotQA (from my memory of the paper; not re-checked here). Only safe for **deterministic subroutines after discovery**, such as paginating a list the model already chose.
- **CodeAct / code-as-action** [P]: the model writes Python or Playwright snippets instead of JSON tool calls, with loops and conditions in one action. The paper reports up to +20% success and fewer turns; those numbers are from my memory of the paper (not re-checked here) and are not web-specific. Risk: weak models write brittle selectors. A safer middle ground [I] is a small DSL of pre-built functions (`for_each_row(list_ref, extract=schema)`, `paginate(ref, until=...)`) that the LLM composes.
- **SkillWeaver** [P]: the agent explores a site, writes Playwright functions, tests them and reuses them. +31.8% relative on WebArena. Needs an exploration phase per site, so it conflicts with "unseen sites" unless done in-run. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.07079
- **Agent Workflow Memory** [P, ICML'25]: induces reusable workflows from past trajectories (offline or online). +51.1% relative on WebArena with fewer steps. Can be applied **site-agnostically**: store abstract workflows like "paginated inbox → filter → open each → extract" rather than click paths. https://arxiv.org/html/2409.07429v1
- **Agentic Plan Caching** [P, 2025]: extracts plan templates from finished runs, matches new tasks by keyword, and a small model adapts the template. -50% cost and -27% latency on average with performance maintained. https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.14852
- **WILBUR** [P]: a ranking model picks in-context demonstrations from earlier runs, plus backtracking. 53% on WebVoyager. Only relevant if you keep a demonstration bank. https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.05902

## 3. AgentOccam in detail (what they removed)

- **Removed:** `noop`; tab operations; `scroll` (full page loaded instead); most `hover` and `press`; limited `goto` and `go_forward`.
- **Changed:** choosing a dropdown option is **one click on the option ID** instead of select-then-choose.
- **Added:** `note`, `stop [answer]`, `go_home`, and `branch` / `prune` over a planning tree.
- **Biggest single jump:** action-space reduction (+11.6 points).
- **Regressions:** pivotal-node history cost 3–6 points on shopping and Reddit.
- **Main takeaway:** a smaller action vocabulary plus a full-page observation in Markdown beats elaborate machinery.
- **For us:** remove any scroll or wait-type tools, and collapse the select-then-choose sequence on cascading selects into one action.

https://arxiv.org/html/2410.13825

## 4. Frameworks: real speed tricks vs hype

- **Stagehand caching** [V]: the cache key is instruction + page content (accessibility tree) + options + URL with tracking parameters stripped. Variables are keyed by *name*, not value. A hit costs zero tokens; a miss means a fresh LLM call. The v3 docs don't describe self-healing, and the "selfHeal" retry exists only in some versions. A cache only pays off across *repeated* runs, which is only useful for us if the eval re-runs the same sites. **Observe→act**: `observe()` returns actions that `act()` replays with no LLM call. https://docs.stagehand.dev/v3/best-practices/caching
- **Skyvern code caching** [V]: records a successful run as Playwright code, replays it with no LLM, and falls back to the agent on breakage. Reported 278.95 s → 119.92 s and $0.11 → $0.04. Same caveat: it needs repeats. https://docs-new.skyvern.com/docs/features/code-caching
- **Notte perception** [V]: flattens the DOM into a labeled action space (interactive elements, form fields, section headings), with a fast heuristic mode and a deep mode. The "86% success" figure is self-reported. https://docs.steel.dev/cookbook/notte
- **AgentQL** [V]: GraphQL-shaped queries (`{ products[] { name price } }`) return JSON or Playwright locators in one call. The useful idea is **schema-shaped extraction requests**; you already have JSON extraction.
- **browser-use `extract`** [V]: a separate cheap LLM call over page Markdown returns only the answer to the main agent. Same as your background extraction.
- **Hype check:** cached replay of any kind (Stagehand, Skyvern) doesn't help on first contact with an unseen site. The real first-visit gains are terse output, prefix caching, batching, and fan-out.

## 5. Speculative and parallel exploration

- **Speculative Actions** [P, ICLR'26]: a fast model guesses the next action, it runs in parallel, and it is committed only on an exact match. Next-action accuracy was 22–38% on τ-bench retail and up to 46% top-3 on HotpotQA. **The headline 20% speedup is from chess, not web.** Only read-only or idempotent actions are safe; orders and submissions are not. https://arxiv.org/html/2510.04371v1
  - Fit for us [I]: speculatively prefetch and extract the links the model is likely to open next (mail rows, Q&A items, spec revisions) in spare tabs. That is lossless and read-only.
- **Tree search (Koh et al.)** [P]: best-first search with an LM value function. +28% relative on WebArena (19.2%) at **much higher** compute. The wrong direction for us. https://arxiv.org/html/2407.01476v4
- **WebDreamer** [P]: the LLM simulates action outcomes before acting. Reported as 4–5x more efficient than tree search, but it still adds calls. Not worth it here.
- **What works:** one LLM call chooses N targets, then code opens them in parallel tabs and extracts with a schema. This is the LLMCompiler pattern applied to browsing.

## 6. One-shot structured extraction

- **Crawl4AI** [V]: HTML → Markdown, then `PruningContentFilter` (`threshold` about 0.4, about 50 ms) produces `fit_markdown`; then schema-based LLM extraction per chunk, with chunks processed in parallel. https://docs.crawl4ai.com/extraction/llm-strategies/
- **ReaderLM-v2** (1.5B, CC BY-NC) [V]: HTML → Markdown/JSON with 98% JSON pass rate. The license blocks commercial use, and it isn't needed when rule-based Markdown conversion is enough.
- **Bottom line:** extract per page (or per chunk) against a schema, not per element. You already do this. Remaining gains [I]: send Markdown, not DOM text, to extraction; deduplicate repeated rows; trim schemas (your X-4 measured -16% output).

## 7. Reported efficiency numbers (for calibration)

| System | Steps / time | Tokens / cost |
|---|---|---|
| AgentOccam | about 9 steps per task | about 2.9k observation tokens per step |
| Steward [P] | 8.5–10 s per step (median) | about $0.028 per step; cache hit 4.8 s |
| BU 1.0 [V] | about 3 s per step, 68 s per task | – |
| Skyvern cached [V] | 120 s per run | $0.04 per run |

Your C version runs about 157 navigation calls with a stable prompt of about 3.1k tokens. A ≤50k-token budget implies roughly 15–25 LLM calls in total, i.e. 6–10x fewer decisions. That is only reachable through fan-out and batching, not through compression alone [I].

---

## Recommended for one day, in order of expected impact

1. **Stop polling with `wait_for`.** The step returns when the next background result arrives. This is your P-3, and it addresses an estimated 18–22 wasted calls per run.
2. **Fan-out tool:** `open_all(refs[], schema)`. One LLM decision opens N model-chosen links in parallel tabs and runs schema extraction. Use it for mail, Q&A and ERP materials. Pattern from LLMCompiler.
3. **Batch actions with a stop-on-DOM-change rule** for navigation, not only forms. Combine extract and then-click (your X-1).
4. **Flash-style output:** no reasoning or evaluation fields, terse action names. Put static prompt plus history first and the fresh observation last, to maximize prefix-cache hits.
5. **AgentOccam pruning:** Markdown tables, one-click dropdown options, no scroll, pivotal-node or diff history (your X-3).
6. **Model-selectable observation modes** (Agent-E): `input_fields` for forms, `text_only` for documents.
7. **Read-only prefetch:** extract likely-next pages in idle tabs before the model asks, committing only on use. Speculative-actions-style, but never for TAN or submit.

Skip for this goal: tree search, WebDreamer, LCoW, fine-tuned rankers, and cache replay (it doesn't help on unseen sites).</result>

**Flash-Searcher** (ICLR 2026): splits the task into a dependency graph (DAG) and runs independent subtasks concurrently. Up to 35% fewer execution steps ("up to", so best case), 67.7% on BrowseComp. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25301

**MindSearch:** the planner writes Python that builds a graph of sub-questions, and searcher agents work on them in parallel. Authors claim 300+ pages in about 3 minutes; this is their own claim. https://arxiv.org/html/2407.20183v2

**Infogent:** Navigator, Extractor and Aggregator agents. The Aggregator spots gaps and decides when to stop. Gains: +7% on FRAMES, +4.3% on AssistantBench. https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.19054

**WebExplorer** is training-data work, not inference speed. It is relevant only as a WebWalkerQA baseline. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06501

**Applying it to your agent:**
- Round 1: send the landing page's deduplicated nav and footer links (`[i] text | href | section`) plus the required schema. One call returns a ranked list of K link indices (e.g. 8–15), not one.
- Open them as concurrent Playwright pages. Run 1 extractor call per page in parallel, each filling only the schema fields it can, with source URL attached.
- Merge the results. If fields are still missing, one more call sees the union of not-yet-visited links from all opened pages and picks the next batch.
- Expect about 2–4 sequential LLM rounds instead of 10–15.
- **Speculative:** no paper benchmarks exactly "pick N links at once from a flat list". The parallel-DAG papers are the closest evidence.

## 2. Filling a form in one call

**Skyvern** has the pattern in its code. Proven: production code. File: `skyvern/core/script_generations/skyvern_page.py`.
- `extract_form_fields()` scans the page in JavaScript with no LLM call. It covers input, select, textarea and ARIA groups, and returns label, type, required flag, placeholder, options, current value and format hint.
- `dynamic_field_map()` makes **one cheap text-only LLM call**: "One LLM call sees ALL fields + ALL data and produces a complete mapping". It uses the prompt `form-field-mapper.j2` and returns `{"1": "John", "2": [...], "3": null}`. Field numbers stand in for IDs.
- Prompt rules: return the EXACT option text and never rephrase it ("I am not a protected veteran", not "No"); reformat values to the field's format hint; leave toggles null by default.
- `fill_from_mapping()` matches options without an LLM (`_match_option`), then makes an AI fallback call only when nothing matches. Native selects use `select_option(label=...)`, retried by value. React-Select style widgets get click, type the value, wait 0.5s, then click the first visible option.
- **Dependent fields:** `fill_multipage_form()` re-scans after filling. If the field count went up ("e.g., State appears after Country"), it makes a second mapping call and fills only fields that were not mapped the first time. Then it clicks Next.
- It detects a stuck page by comparing a signature built from the field labels before and after clicking Next.
- **Weakness:** the re-scan triggers only on *new fields*. A `<select>` that already existed but whose options reloaded is not re-mapped.

**Skyvern's custom dropdowns**, in `skyvern/webeye/actions/handler.py`:
- `sequentially_select_from_dropdown` handles nested menus up to 3 levels (30 for date pickers). It waits for animations to finish between levels.
- `IncrementalScrapePage.start_listen_dom_increment` watches the DOM so the model only sees *newly appeared* option elements.
- `classify_option_match` matches the target text to an option in tiers: exact, then word stem, then substring, then word overlap. Only if that fails does it call a secondary, cheaper LLM with `custom-select.j2`.
- Autocomplete inputs: type the text and look for a match. If none, an LLM suggests 5 candidate values to try. The loop is capped at 1 attempt "to speed up skyvern".

**browser-use** `multi_act` (`browser_use/agent/service.py`): the model returns up to `max_actions_per_step` actions (default 5). The run aborts the rest of the queue when:
- the action has the `terminates_sequence` flag (navigate, search, back, switch tab);
- the URL or focused tab changed after an action;
- an action returned an error.

It does **not** detect DOM changes on the same page, so a dependent select that reloads its options is not caught.

**Stagehand:** one `observe()` returns all field actions, then `act(field)` replays each without an LLM call. The docs claim "2-3x faster". https://docs.stagehand.dev/v3/best-practices/speed-optimization

**Recommended approach for dependent selects.** This is my design, not something a published system does.
- Before filling, find dependency candidates without an LLM: selects with no or placeholder-only options, or `disabled` fields.
- Order of work:
  1. One mapping call for all fields. It should also return the *intended label* for fields whose options have not loaded yet.
  2. Fill in DOM order.
  3. After each select change, wait for the network to go idle or for a MutationObserver to see the next select's option count change.
  4. Match the intended label to the newly loaded options with the deterministic tiered matcher.
  5. Make a fallback LLM call only when nothing matches.
- Typical cost is 1–2 LLM calls per form page.

## 3. Scripts written by the LLM

- **AutoCrawler:** the LLM writes a sequence of XPaths. If extraction fails it steps back up the DOM with "/.." (up to 5 times), then keeps the candidate that works on all 3 seed pages. GPT-4 reached 71.6% correct vs 61.9% with chain-of-thought. The authors estimate it is cheaper than calling an LLM per page once a site has more than 16 pages. https://arxiv.org/html/2404.12753v1
- **CodeAct:** code as the action format gives up to +20% success over JSON or text actions. I could not confirm the "30% fewer steps" figure. https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01030
- **WebAgent** (Gur et al., ICLR 2024): HTML-T5 plans, Flan-U-PaLM writes the program. Over 50% better success on real websites. https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.12856
- **SkillWeaver:** the agent turns practiced tasks into reusable Playwright functions. Reported relative gains are about 31.8% on WebArena and up to 54.3% when weaker agents reuse the skills, and the paper's own figures are inconsistent. https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07079
- **Beyond Browsing:** a hybrid of API calls plus browsing reached 38.9% on WebArena, more than 24 points above browsing alone. https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.16464

**Trade-off:** a script the LLM wrote *is* a navigation decision the LLM made, so it satisfies your rule. The risk is brittleness on sites it has not seen.
- Use it as a *batched action plan* (e.g. "fill these 12 selectors, then return `document.querySelectorAll(...)` text") with guards that hand control back to the LLM.
- Do not use it as an unchecked crawler.
- Running the LLM's JavaScript inside `page.evaluate` needs a sandbox, or at least no credentials in scope.

## 4. Prompt and cache layout

**Manus** (proven in production): https://manus.im/blog/Context-Engineering-for-AI-Agents-Lessons-from-Building-Manus
- Input-to-output token ratio is about 100:1. On Sonnet, cached input costs $0.30/MTok vs $3 uncached (10x).
- Keep the start of the prompt identical across calls (no timestamps) and make history append-only.
- Serialize JSON deterministically; changing key order silently breaks the cache.
- Mask tools through token logits instead of adding or removing them.
- Drop page bodies from context but keep their URLs, so the content can be re-fetched.
- Rewrite a `todo.md` near the end of the context each step so the goal stays in view. Leave errors in the context.

**Qwen (Alibaba Model Studio):** https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/model-studio/context-cache
- Implicit cache: automatic, cache hits cost about 20% of the input price, no hit guarantee.
- Explicit cache: `cache_control` markers, about 10% on hits, 125% to create the entry, 5-minute TTL.
- Minimum 1,024 tokens. qwen-flash supports caching in the Beijing and Singapore regions, but is not on the US explicit-cache list.

**Applying it:** use one fixed system prompt plus the schema as the shared start for all 32 parallel extractor calls, and put the variable page content last. That way the parallel workers reuse the cached start of the prompt.

## 5. Stop as soon as the schema is filled

- WebWalker's Critic and Infogent's Aggregator are the evidence that a sufficiency check helps.
- Cheaper version: do it in Python, with no LLM. Stop when every required field is non-null and its value has been seen on the page (citation check). Each extractor returns `{field: {value, quote, url}}`.
- Spend an LLM call on the stop decision only for conflicting values.
- Skyvern's check for "0 fields mapped, so stop" is a cheap version of the same idea.

## 6. Speculation

- **Speculative Actions** (ICLR 2026): a cheap model guesses the next action and it runs in parallel, kept only if it matches the main model's choice. Up to 55% next-action accuracy, about 20% lossless latency reduction, theoretical ceiling about 50%. Only safe for actions that can be undone or have no side effects (page loads, searches). https://arxiv.org/html/2510.04371v1
- **Dynamic Speculative Planning:** learns online how many steps ahead to speculate, with a cost-latency setting. About 30% lower total cost at similar speed to the fastest lossless method. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.01920

**Assessment:** with about 1s calls and 32 parallel calls, the cheapest speculation is *prefetching*:
- Open the top-K candidate links while the model is still deciding.
- Pre-scrape form fields after every select change.

LLM-on-LLM speculation saves little when each call is already about 1s.

## 7. Benchmarks

- **AgentOccam:** cleaning up the observation and action format alone gave +26.6 points over a plain agent on WebArena. https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13825
- **Agent Workflow Memory:** +51.1% relative success on WebArena, with fewer steps. https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07429
- **CUGA:** 61.7% on WebArena with a planner-executor design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.01861

None of these report wall-clock speed. Leaderboards rank success, not latency, so I found no strong evidence of large speedups from benchmark winners.

## Proven vs speculative

**Proven, worth doing first:**
- Field extraction in JavaScript plus a single mapping call, the Skyvern way.
- Deterministic option matching with an LLM fallback.
- Re-scanning after filling.
- Queues of batched actions that abort when the page changes.
- A stable, append-only prompt layout for caching.

**Plausible but not benchmarked:**
- Picking many links at once from a flat list and opening them in parallel.
- Waiting on DOM changes so a cascade of dependent selects needs no extra LLM call.
- Stopping when the schema is filled, checked in Python.

**Small gains:** LLM-on-LLM speculative actions, about 20%.</result>

"""Entry point (agent.json runs `uv run --no-sync python main.py`), in the sandbox and locally.

Sandbox: attach to the run's browsers (CDP_URLS, one website per browser); never start browsers of our own.
Locally (no CDP_URLS): launch one Chromium with one context per website. Options:
  --out FILE   write answer, trace and evidence as JSON      --dry-run   stop before the binding submission
  --evidence FILE   (dev) skip exploration, replay brief + evidence of an earlier --out file
"""
import argparse
import asyncio
import json
import os
import sys
import time

from playwright.async_api import async_playwright

from rfq import contract
from rfq.agent.orchestrator import Orchestrator
from rfq.browser.site import Site
from rfq.log import log


def cdp_urls() -> list[str]:
    try:
        urls = [u for u in json.loads(os.environ.get("CDP_URLS") or "[]") if isinstance(u, str)]
    except ValueError:
        urls = []
    return urls or ([os.environ["CDP_URL"]] if os.environ.get("CDP_URL") else [])


async def open_sites(playwright, access: list[dict]) -> tuple[dict[str, Site], list]:
    urls, browsers, contexts = cdp_urls(), [], []
    if urls:
        for url in urls:
            browser = await playwright.chromium.connect_over_cdp(url)
            browsers.append(browser)
        for index in range(len(access)):
            browser = browsers[index % len(browsers)]
            if index < len(browsers) and browser.contexts:
                contexts.append(browser.contexts[0])          # the sandbox's own window, recorded by the platform
            else:
                contexts.append(await browser.new_context(viewport={"width": 1280, "height": 800}))
    else:
        browser = await playwright.chromium.launch(headless=os.environ.get("HEADLESS", "1") == "1")
        browsers.append(browser)
        for _ in access:
            contexts.append(await browser.new_context(viewport={"width": 1280, "height": 800}, locale="de-DE"))
    sites = {a["siteId"]: Site(a["siteId"], a["url"], a["credentials"], ctx) for a, ctx in zip(access, contexts)}
    return sites, browsers


STARTED = time.time()


async def main() -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--out")
    parser.add_argument("--dry-run", action="store_true")
    parser.add_argument("--evidence", help="dev only: replay brief + evidence from an earlier --out file")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    if args.dry_run:
        os.environ["RFQ_DRY_RUN"] = "1"
    run, token = contract.load_run()
    log("run", run_id=run.get("run_id"), local=token is None, seconds_left=round(contract.seconds_left(run)),
        sites=[a["siteId"] for a in run["access"]], submission=run.get("submission", {}).get("kind"))
    async with async_playwright() as playwright:
        sites, browsers = await open_sites(playwright, run["access"])
        # A site that cannot be reached at once must not block the others: missions retry it later.
        started = await asyncio.gather(*(asyncio.wait_for(site.start(), timeout=100) for site in sites.values()),
                                       return_exceptions=True)
        for site, outcome in zip(sites.values(), started):
            log("site_ready", site=site.site_id, ok=not isinstance(outcome, Exception),
                error=str(outcome)[:200] if isinstance(outcome, Exception) else None)
        orchestrator = Orchestrator(run, sites, started=STARTED)
        replay = json.load(open(args.evidence)) if args.evidence else None
        try:   # last line of defence: the run ends in time even if something hangs
            result = await asyncio.wait_for(orchestrator.run_all(replay), timeout=max(60, orchestrator.end - time.time() + 45))
        except asyncio.TimeoutError:
            log("watchdog_timeout")
            result = orchestrator.result
        if args.out:
            with open(args.out, "w") as handle:
                json.dump({"answer": result.answer if result else None, "skipped": result.skipped if result else None,
                           "trace": result.trace if result else None, "brief": orchestrator.brief,
                           "status": orchestrator.status, "erp_complete": sorted(orchestrator.erp_complete),
                           "evidence": orchestrator.bb.dump()}, handle, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2, default=str)
        if not cdp_urls():
            for browser in browsers:
                await browser.close()
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    started = time.time()
    try:
        code = asyncio.run(main())
    except Exception as error:   # last resort: log and exit cleanly
        log("fatal", error=f"{type(error).__name__}: {error}"[:1000])
        code = 1
    log("exit", code=code, seconds=round(time.time() - started, 1))
    sys.exit(code)

<result># Research report: making the web agent faster and cheaper without losing accuracy

I checked your `codex/subminute-runtime` branch before writing this. `docs/12-optimization-analysis.md` puts the current version (C) at about 300–430 s and about $0.10 per run. That splits into roughly 157 navigation calls (about 62% of cost), and uncached navigation input alone is about 50% of cost. The docs estimate about 2.5x more navigation decisions than needed, mostly from 18–22 `wait_for` polling calls per run and from separate "extract" and "navigate" steps. The analysis is consistent across sources: **the main lever is fewer navigation decisions, not cheaper tokens.** The recommendations below are ranked with that in mind.

Labels: [P] peer-reviewed paper, [V] vendor-reported, [I] my inference.

---

## 1. Observation compression

| Technique | Mechanism | Reported gain | Fit for us | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **AgentOccam observation simplification** [P, ICLR'25] | Merges static text into the interactive node with the same label. Turns tables and lists into Markdown. Replays only "pivotal nodes" from history (nodes the model names, plus their ancestors, siblings and children). Drops steps from abandoned plan branches. | On a 190-task dev split with GPT-4-Turbo, cumulative success went 14.2 → 25.8 (fewer actions) → 30.0 (no scrolling, full page) → 34.7 (simplified observation) → 36.8 (pivotal history) → 44.2 (planning). **Tokens per step went up** (2210 → 2931) because the whole page is loaded. Steps per task 6.2 → 9.0. | High, and cheap to build. Markdown tables matter a lot for the ERP stock and price-condition grids. Pivotal-node history replaces raw step logs. | https://arxiv.org/html/2410.13825 |
| **Agent-E DOM distillation** [P] | The agent picks one of three DOM views per call: `text_only` (inner text), `input_fields` (compact JSON of interactive elements), `all_fields`. | 73.2% on WebVoyager. No per-mode token numbers. | High. Make the observation mode a tool argument: `input_fields` for forms and the configurator, `text_only` for spec documents and mails. Removes about 14k characters of irrelevant content from many steps [I]. | https://arxiv.org/html/2407.13032v1 |
| **Prune4Web** [P, AAAI'26] | The LLM writes only a `keyword_weights` dict (weights 1–50). A fixed Python template (rapidfuzz plus a stemmer) scores elements by tier (visible text > aria-label/placeholder > class/id) and match type (exact > phrase > word > fuzzy). The top 20 go to the grounder. | 25–50x fewer candidates. Zero-shot GPT-4o-mini filter: Recall@20 89%, grounding 67.6 → 73.8%. Zero-shot GPT-4o Recall@3 is only about 72%. | Medium-high. About 100 lines of Python. Only useful on large pages; our internal sites are probably small. | https://arxiv.org/html/2511.21398 |
| **Mind2Web / MindAct ranking** [P] | A DeBERTa cross-encoder ranks elements and the LLM chooses from the top-k. | A third-party ranker card reports recall@10 of about 93%. | Low. Needs a GPU model and training data, and is overkill for our sites. | https://huggingface.co/torontodeveloper/mind2web-candidate-ranker |
| **WebLINX Dense Markup Ranker** [P] | A dual encoder embeds turn state and elements separately, then ranks by cosine similarity. Cheaper than a cross-encoder. | No isolated recall figure. | Low-medium. BM25 over element text plus attributes gets most of the benefit at no cost [I]. | https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.05930 |
| **D2Snap** [P, 2025] | Downsamples the DOM by merging and averaging subtrees, analogous to JPEG compression, and keeps hierarchy. | 67% vs 65% for a screenshot baseline on Online-Mind2Web at the same token scale. Finding: hierarchy matters. | Medium. Open source (github.com/surfly/D2Snap). Main lesson: keep indentation and hierarchy, don't flatten. | https://arxiv.org/html/2508.04412v2 |
| **LCoW** [P, ICLR'25] | A separate contextualizer LM rewrites the page into a task-relevant summary before the actor sees it. | +15.6 points (closed models) and +23.7 points (open models) on WorkArena. | Adds an LLM call per step, the opposite of our goal. Only helps if the contextualizer replaces several actor steps. | https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.10689 |

Use diffs: "page unchanged except X". | https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01535 |
| **AutoWebGLM, Dripper, SCRIBES** [P] | Rule-based HTML pruning (drop script, style, nav, footer; whitelist attributes). SCRIBES deduplicates repeated siblings. | SCRIBES: about 114k → 17k tokens (-85%) from sibling deduplication. | High for the webmail and Q&A lists: collapse N similar rows to a template plus values, or paginate in code. | https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.01832 |

**Diff observations [I, backed by the 2604.01535 guideline]:** hash each text block. After an action, send only added or changed blocks plus a one-line summary of the rest. This cuts tokens on the many steps where only a dropdown's options change, which is typical of cascading selects.

## 2. Fewer LLM calls (the main lever)

- **Multi-action per step (browser-use `max_actions_per_step`)** [V]: the model outputs a list of actions. The runtime executes them in order and **stops the batch as soon as the page or DOM changes**, then re-observes. That stop rule is what makes batching safe. Your `steps` tool already does this for forms and cut submission from about 51–57 calls to 27. Extend it to navigation, e.g. "open these 5 mail rows, extract each" as one call. https://docs.browser-use.com/customize/agent/all-parameters
- **browser-use `flash_mode`** [V]: "skips evaluation, next goal and thinking and only uses memory." Output shrinks to roughly memory plus action. Their speed post measured output tokens at about 215x the per-token latency of input tokens (1k input = 29 ms; 10 output = 63 ms). They also put **history before the fresh browser state so the prefix stays KV-cacheable**, and keep action names terse (10–15 output tokens). They report about 3 s per step and 68 s per task on Online-Mind2Web for BU 1.0 [V, self-hosted benchmark]. https://browser-use.com/posts/speed-matters
- **Plan-and-Act** [P, ICML'25]: a planner writes high-level steps and an executor grounds them, with replanning after each executor phase. 57.6% on WebArena-Lite, but the gain comes from a fine-tuned planner on synthetic data. A day-sized version: one planner call per site emits a checklist (you already have code checklists), and the executor runs a batch per item. https://arxiv.org/html/2503.09572v3
- **LLMCompiler** [P, ICML'24]: the planner emits a DAG of tool calls and the executor runs independent nodes in parallel. Up to 3.7x lower latency and 6.7x lower cost vs ReAct (best-case, on QA tool tasks, not web). Applies to fan-out: "open these 18 mails / these 6 Q&A pages / these N ERP materials" in parallel tabs from one decision. https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.04511
- **ReWOO** [P, 2023]: plan once with variable placeholders and execute without intermediate observations. The paper reports about 5x token efficiency on HotpotQA (from my memory of the paper; not re-checked here). Only safe for **deterministic subroutines after discovery**, such as paginating a list the model already chose.
- **CodeAct / code-as-action** [P]: the model writes Python or Playwright snippets instead of JSON tool calls, with loops and conditions in one action. The paper reports up to +20% success and fewer turns; those numbers are from my memory of the paper (not re-checked here) and are not web-specific. Risk: weak models write brittle selectors. A safer middle ground [I] is a small DSL of pre-built functions (`for_each_row(list_ref, extract=schema)`, `paginate(ref, until=...)`) that the LLM composes.
- **SkillWeaver** [P]: the agent explores a site, writes Playwright functions, tests them and reuses them. +31.8% relative on WebArena. Needs an exploration phase per site, so it conflicts with "unseen sites" unless done in-run. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.07079
- **Agent Workflow Memory** [P, ICML'25]: induces reusable workflows from past trajectories (offline or online). +51.1% relative on WebArena with fewer steps. Can be applied **site-agnostically**: store abstract workflows like "paginated inbox → filter → open each → extract" rather than click paths. https://arxiv.org/html/2409.07429v1
- **Agentic Plan Caching** [P, 2025]: extracts plan templates from finished runs, matches new tasks by keyword, and a small model adapts the template. -50% cost and -27% latency on average with performance maintained. https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.14852
- **WILBUR** [P]: a ranking model picks in-context demonstrations from earlier runs, plus backtracking. 53% on WebVoyager. Only relevant if you keep a demonstration bank. https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.05902

## 3. AgentOccam in detail (what they removed)

- **Removed:** `noop`; tab operations; `scroll` (full page loaded instead); most `hover` and `press`; limited `goto` and `go_forward`.
- **Changed:** choosing a dropdown option is **one click on the option ID** instead of select-then-choose.
- **Added:** `note`, `stop [answer]`, `go_home`, and `branch` / `prune` over a planning tree.
- **Biggest single jump:** action-space reduction (+11.6 points).
- **Regressions:** pivotal-node history cost 3–6 points on shopping and Reddit.
- **Main takeaway:** a smaller action vocabulary plus a full-page observation in Markdown beats elaborate machinery.
- **For us:** remove any scroll or wait-type tools, and collapse the select-then-choose sequence on cascading selects into one action.

https://arxiv.org/html/2410.13825

## 4. Frameworks: real speed tricks vs hype

- **Stagehand caching** [V]: the cache key is instruction + page content (accessibility tree) + options + URL with tracking parameters stripped. Variables are keyed by *name*, not value. A hit costs zero tokens; a miss means a fresh LLM call. The v3 docs don't describe self-healing, and the "selfHeal" retry exists only in some versions. A cache only pays off across *repeated* runs, which is only useful for us if the eval re-runs the same sites. **Observe→act**: `observe()` returns actions that `act()` replays with no LLM call. https://docs.stagehand.dev/v3/best-practices/caching
- **Skyvern code caching** [V]: records a successful run as Playwright code, replays it with no LLM, and falls back to the agent on breakage. Reported 278.95 s → 119.92 s and $0.11 → $0.04. Same caveat: it needs repeats. https://docs-new.skyvern.com/docs/features/code-caching
- **Notte perception** [V]: flattens the DOM into a labeled action space (interactive elements, form fields, section headings), with a fast heuristic mode and a deep mode. The "86% success" figure is self-reported. https://docs.steel.dev/cookbook/notte
- **AgentQL** [V]: GraphQL-shaped queries (`{ products[] { name price } }`) return JSON or Playwright locators in one call. The useful idea is **schema-shaped extraction requests**; you already have JSON extraction.
- **browser-use `extract`** [V]: a separate cheap LLM call over page Markdown returns only the answer to the main agent. Same as your background extraction.
- **Hype check:** cached replay of any kind (Stagehand, Skyvern) doesn't help on first contact with an unseen site. The real first-visit gains are terse output, prefix caching, batching, and fan-out.

## 5. Speculative and parallel exploration

- **Speculative Actions** [P, ICLR'26]: a fast model guesses the next action, it runs in parallel, and it is committed only on an exact match. Next-action accuracy was 22–38% on τ-bench retail and up to 46% top-3 on HotpotQA. **The headline 20% speedup is from chess, not web.** Only read-only or idempotent actions are safe; orders and submissions are not. https://arxiv.org/html/2510.04371v1
  - Fit for us [I]: speculatively prefetch and extract the links the model is likely to open next (mail rows, Q&A items, spec revisions) in spare tabs. That is lossless and read-only.
- **Tree search (Koh et al.)** [P]: best-first search with an LM value function. +28% relative on WebArena (19.2%) at **much higher** compute. The wrong direction for us. https://arxiv.org/html/2407.01476v4
- **WebDreamer** [P]: the LLM simulates action outcomes before acting. Reported as 4–5x more efficient than tree search, but it still adds calls. Not worth it here.
- **What works:** one LLM call chooses N targets, then code opens them in parallel tabs and extracts with a schema. This is the LLMCompiler pattern applied to browsing.

## 6. One-shot structured extraction

- **Crawl4AI** [V]: HTML → Markdown, then `PruningContentFilter` (`threshold` about 0.4, about 50 ms) produces `fit_markdown`; then schema-based LLM extraction per chunk, with chunks processed in parallel. https://docs.crawl4ai.com/extraction/llm-strategies/
- **ReaderLM-v2** (1.5B, CC BY-NC) [V]: HTML → Markdown/JSON with 98% JSON pass rate. The license blocks commercial use, and it isn't needed when rule-based Markdown conversion is enough.
- **Bottom line:** extract per page (or per chunk) against a schema, not per element. You already do this. Remaining gains [I]: send Markdown, not DOM text, to extraction; deduplicate repeated rows; trim schemas (your X-4 measured -16% output).

## 7. Reported efficiency numbers (for calibration)

| System | Steps / time | Tokens / cost |
|---|---|---|
| AgentOccam | about 9 steps per task | about 2.9k observation tokens per step |
| Steward [P] | 8.5–10 s per step (median) | about $0.028 per step; cache hit 4.8 s |
| BU 1.0 [V] | about 3 s per step, 68 s per task | – |
| Skyvern cached [V] | 120 s per run | $0.04 per run |

Your C version runs about 157 navigation calls with a stable prompt of about 3.1k tokens. A ≤50k-token budget implies roughly 15–25 LLM calls in total, i.e. 6–10x fewer decisions. That is only reachable through fan-out and batching, not through compression alone [I].

---

## Recommended for one day, in order of expected impact

1. **Stop polling with `wait_for`.** The step returns when the next background result arrives. This is your P-3, and it addresses an estimated 18–22 wasted calls per run.
2. **Fan-out tool:** `open_all(refs[], schema)`. One LLM decision opens N model-chosen links in parallel tabs and runs schema extraction. Use it for mail, Q&A and ERP materials. Pattern from LLMCompiler.
3. **Batch actions with a stop-on-DOM-change rule** for navigation, not only forms. Combine extract and then-click (your X-1).
4. **Flash-style output:** no reasoning or evaluation fields, terse action names. Put static prompt plus history first and the fresh observation last, to maximize prefix-cache hits.
5. **AgentOccam pruning:** Markdown tables, one-click dropdown options, no scroll, pivotal-node or diff history (your X-3).
6. **Model-selectable observation modes** (Agent-E): `input_fields` for forms, `text_only` for documents.
7. **Read-only prefetch:** extract likely-next pages in idle tabs before the model asks, committing only on use. Speculative-actions-style, but never for TAN or submit.

Skip for this goal: tree search, WebDreamer, LCoW, fine-tuned rankers, and cache replay (it doesn't help on unseen sites).</result>

## 1. Show all links at once and open several in parallel

**WebWalker** (arXiv 2501.07572): proven, but it is not a speedup.
- **Mechanism:** each step, the Explorer sees the page as markdown plus a list of clickable buttons with their URLs (extracted with BeautifulSoup) and picks one subpage, up to 15 steps. After each step a Critic records whether the page was useful and whether the info is now sufficient, and answers when it is.
- **Gains:** accuracy only. GPT-4o went from 33.8 (ReAct) to 37.5, at slightly more actions (4.67 vs 3.83). Strategy matters less than letting a small model see the whole link set cheaply.
- https://arxiv.org/html/2501.07572v3

**Flash-Searcher** (ICLR 2026): splits the task into a dependency graph (DAG) and runs independent subtasks concurrently. Up to 35% fewer execution steps ("up to", so best case), 67.7% on BrowseComp. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25301

**MindSearch:** the planner writes Python that builds a graph of sub-questions, and searcher agents work on them in parallel. Authors claim 300+ pages in about 3 minutes; this is their own claim. https://arxiv.org/html/2407.20183v2

**Infogent:** Navigator, Extractor and Aggregator agents. The Aggregator spots gaps and decides when to stop. Gains: +7% on FRAMES, +4.3% on AssistantBench. https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.19054

**WebExplorer** is training-data work, not inference speed. It is relevant only as a WebWalkerQA baseline. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06501

**Applying it to your agent:**
- Round 1: send the landing page's deduplicated nav and footer links (`[i] text | href | section`) plus the required schema. One call returns a ranked list of K link indices (e.g. 8–15), not one.
- Open them as concurrent Playwright pages. Run 1 extractor call per page in parallel, each filling only the schema fields it can, with source URL attached.
- Merge the results. If fields are still missing, one more call sees the union of not-yet-visited links from all opened pages and picks the next batch.
- Expect about 2–4 sequential LLM rounds instead of 10–15.
- **Speculative:** no paper benchmarks exactly "pick N links at once from a flat list". The parallel-DAG papers are the closest evidence.

## 2. Filling a form in one call

**Skyvern** has the pattern in its code. Proven: production code. File: `skyvern/core/script_generations/skyvern_page.py`.
- `extract_form_fields()` scans the page in JavaScript with no LLM call. It covers input, select, textarea and ARIA groups, and returns label, type, required flag, placeholder, options, current value and format hint.
- `dynamic_field_map()` makes **one cheap text-only LLM call**: "One LLM call sees ALL fields + ALL data and produces a complete mapping". It uses the prompt `form-field-mapper.j2` and returns `{"1": "John", "2": [...], "3": null}`. Field numbers stand in for IDs.
- Prompt rules: return the EXACT option text and never rephrase it ("I am not a protected veteran", not "No"); reformat values to the field's format hint; leave toggles null by default.
- `fill_from_mapping()` matches options without an LLM (`_match_option`), then makes an AI fallback call only when nothing matches. Native selects use `select_option(label=...)`, retried by value. React-Select style widgets get click, type the value, wait 0.5s, then click the first visible option.
- **Dependent fields:** `fill_multipage_form()` re-scans after filling. If the field count went up ("e.g., State appears after Country"), it makes a second mapping call and fills only fields that were not mapped the first time. Then it clicks Next.
- It detects a stuck page by comparing a signature built from the field labels before and after clicking Next.
- **Weakness:** the re-scan triggers only on *new fields*. A `<select>` that already existed but whose options reloaded is not re-mapped.

**Skyvern's custom dropdowns**, in `skyvern/webeye/actions/handler.py`:
- `sequentially_select_from_dropdown` handles nested menus up to 3 levels (30 for date pickers). It waits for animations to finish between levels.
- `IncrementalScrapePage.start_listen_dom_increment` watches the DOM so the model only sees *newly appeared* option elements.
- `classify_option_match` matches the target text to an option in tiers: exact, then word stem, then substring, then word overlap. Only if that fails does it call a secondary, cheaper LLM with `custom-select.j2`.
- Autocomplete inputs: type the text and look for a match. If none, an LLM suggests 5 candidate values to try. The loop is capped at 1 attempt "to speed up skyvern".

**browser-use** `multi_act` (`browser_use/agent/service.py`): the model returns up to `max_actions_per_step` actions (default 5). The run aborts the rest of the queue when:
- the action has the `terminates_sequence` flag (navigate, search, back, switch tab);
- the URL or focused tab changed after an action;
- an action returned an error.

It does **not** detect DOM changes on the same page, so a dependent select that reloads its options is not caught.

**Stagehand:** one `observe()` returns all field actions, then `act(field)` replays each without an LLM call. The docs claim "2-3x faster". https://docs.stagehand.dev/v3/best-practices/speed-optimization

**Recommended approach for dependent selects.** This is my design, not something a published system does.
- Before filling, find dependency candidates without an LLM: selects with no or placeholder-only options, or `disabled` fields.
- Order of work:
  1. One mapping call for all fields. It should also return the *intended label* for fields whose options have not loaded yet.
  2. Fill in DOM order.
  3. After each select change, wait for the network to go idle or for a MutationObserver to see the next select's option count change.
  4. Match the intended label to the newly loaded options with the deterministic tiered matcher.
  5. Make a fallback LLM call only when nothing matches.
- Typical cost is 1–2 LLM calls per form page.

## 3. Scripts written by the LLM

- **AutoCrawler:** the LLM writes a sequence of XPaths. If extraction fails it steps back up the DOM with "/.." (up to 5 times), then keeps the candidate that works on all 3 seed pages. GPT-4 reached 71.6% correct vs 61.9% with chain-of-thought. The authors estimate it is cheaper than calling an LLM per page once a site has more than 16 pages. https://arxiv.org/html/2404.12753v1
- **CodeAct:** code as the action format gives up to +20% success over JSON or text actions. I could not confirm the "30% fewer steps" figure. https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01030
- **WebAgent** (Gur et al., ICLR 2024): HTML-T5 plans, Flan-U-PaLM writes the program. Over 50% better success on real websites. https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.12856
- **SkillWeaver:** the agent turns practiced tasks into reusable Playwright functions. Reported relative gains are about 31.8% on WebArena and up to 54.3% when weaker agents reuse the skills, and the paper's own figures are inconsistent. https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07079
- **Beyond Browsing:** a hybrid of API calls plus browsing reached 38.9% on WebArena, more than 24 points above browsing alone. https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.16464

**Trade-off:** a script the LLM wrote *is* a navigation decision the LLM made, so it satisfies your rule. The risk is brittleness on sites it has not seen.
- Use it as a *batched action plan* (e.g. "fill these 12 selectors, then return `document.querySelectorAll(...)` text") with guards that hand control back to the LLM.
- Do not use it as an unchecked crawler.
- Running the LLM's JavaScript inside `page.evaluate` needs a sandbox, or at least no credentials in scope.

## 4. Prompt and cache layout

**Manus** (proven in production): https://manus.im/blog/Context-Engineering-for-AI-Agents-Lessons-from-Building-Manus
- Input-to-output token ratio is about 100:1. On Sonnet, cached input costs $0.30/MTok vs $3 uncached (10x).
- Keep the start of the prompt identical across calls (no timestamps) and make history append-only.
- Serialize JSON deterministically; changing key order silently breaks the cache.
- Mask tools through token logits instead of adding or removing them.
- Drop page bodies from context but keep their URLs, so the content can be re-fetched.
- Rewrite a `todo.md` near the end of the context each step so the goal stays in view. Leave errors in the context.

**Qwen (Alibaba Model Studio):** https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/model-studio/context-cache
- Implicit cache: automatic, cache hits cost about 20% of the input price, no hit guarantee.
- Explicit cache: `cache_control` markers, about 10% on hits, 125% to create the entry, 5-minute TTL.
- Minimum 1,024 tokens. qwen-flash supports caching in the Beijing and Singapore regions, but is not on the US explicit-cache list.

**Applying it:** use one fixed system prompt plus the schema as the shared start for all 32 parallel extractor calls, and put the variable page content last. That way the parallel workers reuse the cached start of the prompt.

## 5. Stop as soon as the schema is filled

- WebWalker's Critic and Infogent's Aggregator are the evidence that a sufficiency check helps.
- Cheaper version: do it in Python, with no LLM. Stop when every required field is non-null and its value has been seen on the page (citation check). Each extractor returns `{field: {value, quote, url}}`.
- Spend an LLM call on the stop decision only for conflicting values.
- Skyvern's check for "0 fields mapped, so stop" is a cheap version of the same idea.

## 6. Speculation

- **Speculative Actions** (ICLR 2026): a cheap model guesses the next action and it runs in parallel, kept only if it matches the main model's choice. Up to 55% next-action accuracy, about 20% lossless latency reduction, theoretical ceiling about 50%. Only safe for actions that can be undone or have no side effects (page loads, searches). https://arxiv.org/html/2510.04371v1
- **Dynamic Speculative Planning:** learns online how many steps ahead to speculate, with a cost-latency setting. About 30% lower total cost at similar speed to the fastest lossless method. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.01920

**Assessment:** with about 1s calls and 32 parallel calls, the cheapest speculation is *prefetching*:
- Open the top-K candidate links while the model is still deciding.
- Pre-scrape form fields after every select change.

LLM-on-LLM speculation saves little when each call is already about 1s.

## 7. Benchmarks

- **AgentOccam:** cleaning up the observation and action format alone gave +26.6 points over a plain agent on WebArena. https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13825
- **Agent Workflow Memory:** +51.1% relative success on WebArena, with fewer steps. https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07429
- **CUGA:** 61.7% on WebArena with a planner-executor design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.01861

None of these report wall-clock speed. Leaderboards rank success, not latency, so I found no strong evidence of large speedups from benchmark winners.

## Proven vs speculative

**Proven, worth doing first:**
- Field extraction in JavaScript plus a single mapping call, the Skyvern way.
- Deterministic option matching with an LLM fallback.
- Re-scanning after filling.
- Queues of batched actions that abort when the page changes.
- A stable, append-only prompt layout for caching.

**Plausible but not benchmarked:**
- Picking many links at once from a flat list and opening them in parallel.
- Waiting on DOM changes so a cascade of dependent selects needs no extra LLM call.
- Stopping when the schema is filled, checked in Python.

**Small gains:** LLM-on-LLM speculative actions, about 20%.</result>

1. **Stop polling with `wait_for`.** The step returns when the next background result arrives. This is your P-3, and it addresses an estimated 18–22 wasted calls per run.

**MindSearch:** the planner writes Python that builds a graph of sub-questions, and searcher agents work on them in parallel. Authors claim 300+ pages in about 3 minutes; this is their own claim. https://arxiv.org/html/2407.20183v2

- Open them as concurrent Playwright pages. Run 1 extractor call per page in parallel, each filling only the schema fields it can, with source URL attached.

- Expect about 2–4 sequential LLM rounds instead of 10–15.

- `dynamic_field_map()` makes **one cheap text-only LLM call**: "One LLM call sees ALL fields + ALL data and produces a complete mapping". It uses the prompt `form-field-mapper.j2` and returns `{"1": "John", "2": [...], "3": null}`. Field numbers stand in for IDs.

  4. Match the intended label to the newly loaded options with the deterministic tiered matcher.

Up to 55% next-action accuracy, about 20% lossless latency reduction, theoretical ceiling about 50%. Only safe for actions that can be undone or have no side effects (page loads, searches). https://arxiv.org/html/2510.04371v1
- **Dynamic Speculative Planning:** learns online how many steps ahead to speculate, with a cost-latency setting. About 30% lower total cost at similar speed to the fastest lossless method. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.01920

**Assessment:** with about 1s calls and 32 parallel calls, the cheapest speculation is *prefetching*:
- Open the top-K candidate links while the model is still deciding.
- Pre-scrape form fields after every select change.

LLM-on-LLM speculation saves little when each call is already about 1s.

## 7. Benchmarks

- **AgentOccam:** cleaning up the observation and action format alone gave +26.6 points over a plain agent on WebArena. https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13825
- **Agent Workflow Memory:** +51.1% relative success on WebArena, with fewer steps. https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07429
- **CUGA:** 61.7% on WebArena with a planner-executor design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.01861

None of these report wall-clock speed. Leaderboards rank success, not latency, so I found no strong evidence of large speedups from benchmark winners.

## Proven vs speculative

**Proven, worth doing first:**
- Field extraction in JavaScript plus a single mapping call, the Skyvern way.
- Deterministic option matching with an LLM fallback.
- Re-scanning after filling.
- Queues of batched actions that abort when the page changes.
- A stable, append-only prompt layout for caching.

**Plausible but not benchmarked:**
- Picking many links at once from a flat list and opening them in parallel.
- Waiting on DOM changes so a cascade of dependent selects needs no extra LLM call.
- Stopping when the schema is filled, checked in Python.

**Small gains:** LLM-on-LLM speculative actions, about 20%.</result>

### 2.1 Ablauf und Abhängigkeiten

```

run_all (orchestrator.py:573)

 │                               bekannt (:498-509), eigener Tab je Gruppe (on_new_tab), background_extraction
 ├─ resolve (:559)               deterministische Regeln (rules/resolve.py), Trace

```

**Explorer** (`explorer.py:153-231`): ein Tool pro Schritt.
- Prompt aus System + Tools, Mission-Intro, „STEPS SO FAR“ (letzte 20 Zeilen, `:185`), letztes Ergebnis (≤ 3.000 Zeichen), Hintergrund-Ergebnisse, Checkliste, Beobachtung (≤ 14.000 Zeichen, `site.py:20`).
- Loop-Schutz über die Signatur Aktion + Beobachtung (`:197-219`).
- Die Mission endet, sobald die Code-Checkliste vollständig ist (`:168-176`).

**Hintergrund-Extraktion** (`explorer.py:270-299`): `extract`/`extract_urls` laufen als Task.

### 2.4 Bekannte Korrektheits- und Generalisierungsprobleme

1. **Zwei Rollen auf derselben Site** (`orchestrator.py:422-424`, `:486`):
   - `site_for(role)` liefert dasselbe `Site`-Objekt. Zwei Explorer arbeiten dann gleichzeitig auf *einem* Tab mit wechselnden Refs.
   - Privat realistisch: Laut Plattform-Regeln ist die Information „anders verteilt“, etwa ein Lastenheft als Dokument im Vergabeportal.
2. **Keine Suche auf einer anderen Site** (W03 offen, `docs/11`):
   - Findet z. B. die Spezifikations-Mission keine Anforderungen, startet keine ERP-Mission, weil `erp_groups` die Anforderungen braucht (`:533-539`).
   - Folge: kein Material → `no_bid`. `recheck_no_bid` liest nur die Q&A neu (`:429-461`).
   - Ein solches falsches `no_bid` kostet ≈ 85–95 Punkte.
3. **Hintergrund-Extraktion verzögert Rückmeldungen:**
   - Das Modell sieht „NOTHING of kind …“ oder Ladefehler einen oder zwei Schritte später.
   - Auf unbekannten Layouts kann das Umwege erzeugen; auf public nicht beobachtet.
   - Es gibt keinen Schalter, um sie ohne Codeänderung abzuschalten (fest `True`, `:414`, `:555`).
4. **Doppelte Mail-Extraktionen:** 22–30 `mail_message` pro Run bei ≈ 19 relevanten Nachrichten [gemessen, `evidence_done.kinds`].
5. **Beobachtbarkeit:** Die Frühphase ist in Sandbox-Runs nicht einsehbar (§3.6).

### 4.1 Kernbegründungen der wichtigsten Urteile

**A3 Planner/Executor:**
- Unsere Missionen sind kurz (15–30 Schritte) und reaktiv: Links und Gates zeigen sich erst auf der Seite.
- Ein Plan spart nur, wenn er stimmt. Auf unbekannten Layouts muss der Executor jeden Plan-Schritt an ein Element binden. Das braucht wieder ein Modell oder unscharfes Matching (Fehlerquelle).
- Ein Executor ohne Modell grenzt zudem an den verbotenen „festen Klickpfad“.
- Der Kern des Vorteils, mehrere Aktionen pro Entscheidung, lässt sich mit A6 lokal holen, ohne Umbau.

**A11 Clef:**
- Ein Navigations-Call kostet hier ≈ $0.00044, weil 3.136 Tokens gecacht sind. Clef kostet $0.24/M ohne Cache-Rabatt.
- Kosten-Break-even: Zustand < Akzeptanzrate × ≈ 1.830 Tokens. Real liegen die Zustände bei ≥ 2.000 Tokens.
- Die meisten Schritte brauchen Argumente (URL-Listen, Formularwerte), die ein Entscheidungsmodell nicht liefern kann. Es käme also ein Call *hinzu*.

**A15:**
- Verlagert die Extraktion auf den kritischen Pfad, denn Output-Tokens sind seriell: 21 ms/Token.
- Bricht die Parallelität, die C gerade erst gewonnen hat.

**A14:** scheitert an Fair Play und am privaten Konfigurator, der anders aussieht.

### 4.2 Wechselwirkungen und Verschiebung des kritischen Pfads

- **Hintergrund-Extraktion hat Slot-Druck und Warteschleifen erzeugt.**
  - P-3 (Warten auf Ergebnisse statt `wait_for`-Schleifen) und P-4 (Lanes) sind die direkte Korrektur.
  - Ohne P-3 verbraucht A6 (`then_click`) zusätzliche Slots schneller. Daher kommt P-3 vor X-1.
- **Verschiebung des kritischen Pfads:**
  - Wird ERP um 20–30 s schneller, wird in manchen Runs Mail kritisch (Ende bis 267 s, `run_fef81…`). X-1/X-2 gelten deshalb für ERP *und* Mail.
  - Danach dominieren Spezifikations-Gate (≈ 85 s) und Abgabe (≈ 80 s). Deshalb ist zuerst die Messung O-1 nötig, sonst fehlt für X-6 die Grundlage.

5	Dieses Dokument liefert die Begründung.

13	
14	## 0. Kurzfassung
15	
16	- **Stand:** Die aktuelle Version C liegt auf dem Leaderboard auf Platz 1: Qualität 100, eligible, Kosten × Zeit 31,1 $·s; Platz 2 liegt bei 49,7.
17	  - Vier Sandbox-Runs von C: 299–431 s, $0.100–0.110, C×T 31,1–47,5 (Median 33,2).
18	  - Die Streuung innerhalb *eines* Pakets ist größer als die meisten Einzeleffekte. Jede Entscheidung braucht deshalb gepaarte Wiederholungen.
19	- **Kosten:** Navigations-Calls kosten ≈ 62 % (≈ 157 Calls à ≈ $0.00044). Ungecachter Navigations-Input allein macht ≈ 50 % der Gesamtkosten aus. Extraktionen kosten ≈ 38 %.
20	  - Der größte Hebel ist die **Zahl der Navigationsschritte**, nicht der Preis pro Token.
21	  - Grob 2,5× mehr Navigationsentscheidungen als nötig. Die Treiber: 18–22 `wait_for` pro Run als Warteschleife auf Hintergrund-Extraktionen, getrennte Schritte für „extrahieren“ und „weiter navigieren“, wiederholte Gates und Suchen pro Tab.
22	- **Laufzeit, kritischer Pfad:**
23	
24	  | Abschnitt | Dauer |
25	  |---|---|
26	  | Brief | ≈ 13–17 s |
27	  | Spezifikation bis Anforderungen (ERP-Start bei ≈ 100 s) | ≈ 85 s, in der Sandbox nicht messbar |
28	  | ERP, langsamste Gruppe | ≈ 110–140 s |
29	  | Abgabe | ≈ 72–90 s |
30	
31	- **Neue Nebenwirkungen der Hintergrund-Extraktion:**
32	  - Die 10 Modell-Slots sind 14–62 s pro Run voll belegt; Navigations-Calls warten hinter Extraktionen.
33	  - Hedging verdoppelt gesunde, nur lange Calls; verlorene Zwillinge werden mit abgerechnet.
34	- **Blinder Fleck:** Die Plattform behält nur die letzten 256 stdout-Zeilen. Die ersten ≈ 100 s jedes Sandbox-Runs sind unsichtbar.
35	- **Robustheitslücken für den privaten Datensatz:** Dort sind die Informationen laut Plattform anders verteilt.
36	  - Es fehlt eine gezielte Suche fehlender Evidenz auf einer anderen Site.
37	  - Zwei Rollen auf derselben Site teilen sich einen Tab.
38	  - Es gibt keine Perturbations-Tests.
39	- **Entscheidung:** Die bestehende Architektur gezielt optimieren und zuerst Mess- und Robustheits-Gates einziehen. Kein Umbau. Clef, Frontier-Modelle und eine Planner/Executor-Neuarchitektur bringen keinen belastbaren Vorteil.
40	- **Erwarteter Korridor nach der Roadmap [Schätzung]:**
41	  - Median C×T ≈ 33 → **≈ 23** (zentral; ≈ 285 s, ≈ $0.081)
42	  - optimistisch ≈ 17, pessimistisch ≈ 31
43	  - Qualität und Eligibility sind Bedingung, nicht Teil der Rechnung.

45	## 1. Datengrundlage und Methode
46	
47	| Quelle | Inhalt | Grenzen |
48	|---|---|---|
49	| `GET /v1/runs/{id}` | offizielle Zeit (`score.duration_ms`), Kosten, Qualität, Eligibility, Paket | keine |
50	| `GET /v1/runs/{id}/llm-calls` | jeder Modell-Call: Start, Latenz, `queue_ms`, Tokens (ungecacht/gecacht/Output), Kosten, Status | kein Tag der Mission; `queue_ms` ≈ Latenz − 0,3 s, daher als Wartezeit unbrauchbar [unverifiziert] |
51	| `GET /v1/runs/{id}/logs.jsonl` | unsere JSON-Zeilen | nur die letzten 256 stdout-Zeilen pro Run (§3.6) |
52	| `dev/runs/n123.log` | vollständiges lokales Log (Version B, Scouting-Sites) | lokales Netz instabil (`ERR_NETWORK_CHANGED`, Proxy-Timeouts): nur für Abläufe, nicht für Zeiten |
53	| Lokale Cache-Probe über `atira models proxy` | gecachte Tokens bei wachsendem stabilem Präfix | Dienst lieferte während der Probe Timeouts und 500er |
54	
55	**Klassifikation der Calls:**
56	- **Navigation:** Prompt einschließlich Cache ≥ 3.300 Tokens. Das sind System-Prompt + Tools ≈ 3.136 Tokens plus Inhalt; darunter fallen auch `steps`-Calls der Abgabe.
57	- **Extraktion:** alle übrigen Calls (JSON-Modus). Der Brief zählt dazu.

62	- **C:** zusätzlich Hintergrund-Extraktion für ERP/Mail und parallele ERP-Tabs (`006bc96`, Paket `d4e94c07f4b3`)

107	| Code-Checklisten mit Auto-Abschluss | jede Mission endet am Checklistenende (`mission_complete`-Events in allen C-Runs) |

119	  - Extraktion über separate JSON-Calls ohne Thinking (`orchestrator.py:27`, Default aus)

127	1. **Zwei Rollen auf derselben Site** (`orchestrator.py:422-424`, `:486`):
128	   - `site_for(role)` liefert dasselbe `Site`-Objekt. Zwei Explorer arbeiten dann gleichzeitig auf *einem* Tab mit wechselnden Refs.

376	### 5.3 Break-even-Bedingungen
377	
378	**Hedging:** Ein Zwilling kostet einen vollen Call (c ≈ $0.0006 = 0,58 % von C). Er lohnt sich, wenn
379	
380	    s · Δ · k / T  ≥  c / C
381	
382	- s = Anteil der gehedgten Calls, die sonst bis zum Timeout hängen
383	- Δ = gesparte Sekunden: 60 − 12 = 48 s für Navigation
384	- k = Wahrscheinlichkeit, auf dem kritischen Pfad zu liegen, ≈ 0,5
385	
386	**Ergebnis:** s ≥ 0,0058 · 326 / (48 · 0,5) ≈ **0,08**.
387	- Heute hängt praktisch keiner der gehedgten Calls (alle gesund, nur lang), also s ≈ 0.
388	- Hedging lohnt nur mit Schwellen, die gesunde lange Calls nicht treffen (P-1).
389	
390	**Lanes:** Kosten 0. Lohnt, wenn die lokale Slot-Wartezeit für Navigation > 0 ist *und* höhere Parallelität die Latenz pro Call nicht erhöht.
391	- **Entscheidung:** Navigations-Slot-Wartezeit −50 %, Navigations-p50 nicht über +10 %.
392	- Teamlimit: 32 Slots über alle Runs; 16 pro Run lassen Platz für einen zweiten Run.
393	
394	**Recovery auf anderer Site (G-2):**
395	- **Kosten nur bei Lücken:** ≈ $0.005–0.01 und ≤ 150 s.
396	- **Gewinn bei Erfolg:** typischerweise 5 Punkte (Rabatt) bis ≈ 90 Punkte (kein Material → `no_bid`).
397	- Qualität ist lexikografisch vorrangig, deshalb lohnt es immer, solange die Abgabe rechtzeitig bleibt. Recovery nur, wenn ≥ 120 s bis zum Evidenzende bleiben.
398	
399	**Router oder Verifier mit kleinerem Modell:** Er ersetzt den großen Call nur, wenn seine Entscheidung *ohne* den großen Call ausführbar ist.
400	- In unserem Loop tragen ≈ 80 % der Schritte Argumente: Refs, URL-Listen, Formularwerte.
401	- Ein Router *ergänzt* dann den großen Call. Kosten-Break-even für Clef: Zustand < Akzeptanzrate × 1.830 Tokens.
402	- Ein Verifier verdoppelt die betroffenen Calls. Er lohnt nur, wenn p(Fehler) × Punktverlust die Qualitätsdifferenz zur nächsten Teamplatzierung bedroht. Kein Tempo-Instrument.
403	
404	**Parallele Requests** (spekulativ zwei Varianten): kosten 2×. Lohnen nur bei Hängern (siehe Hedging). Nicht empfohlen.
405	
406	### 5.4 Messungen, die Entscheidungen kippen würden
407	
408	| Wenn … | dann … |
409	|---|---|
410	| O-1 zeigt Navigations-Slot-Wartezeit < 5 s pro Run | P-4 entfällt (Lanes bleiben aus) |
411	| O-1 zeigt Spezifikation bis Anforderungen ≤ 45 s nach dem Brief | X-6 entfällt; Fokus auf ERP/Mail |
412	| O-1 zeigt Historie < 25 % der Prompt-Zeichen | X-3 entfällt |
413	| Paarvergleich zeigt bei X-1 Schleifen oder falsche Klicks (mehr blockierte Wiederholungen) | X-1 aus |
414	| Offline-Replay zeigt < 100 % Feldübereinstimmung bei gekürztem Schema | X-4 für diese Art aus |
415	| Hängerrate steigt wieder (Plattformlast) | P-1-Schwellen nur für lange Calls anheben, Hedging nie ganz entfernen |
416	| Perturbations-Tests (G-3) scheitern am Serializer | erst dort reparieren, Tempo-Schritte zurückstellen |
417	
418	## 6. Architekturentscheidung
419	
420	**Gewählt:** gezielte Optimierung der bestehenden Architektur (A2), in der Reihenfolge
421	1. Messbarkeit (O)
422	2. Robustheits-Gates (G)
423	3. risikoarme Tempo-Schritte (P)
424	4. Experimente mit festem Entscheidungsablauf (X)
425	
426	**Begründung gegen die stärksten Alternativen:**
427	- **Gegen Planner/Executor (A3):** Der Vorteil (weniger Entscheidungen) lässt sich mit Aktionspaketen (A6) lokal und reversibel erreichen. Die Kosten des Umbaus und das Generalisierungsrisiko auf unbekannten Layouts sind hoch. Der Nutzen ist nicht belegt.
428	- **Gegen Clef und Mischmodelle (A11):** Ein Navigations-Call ist hier dank Cache billiger als ein Clef-Call. Die meisten Schritte brauchen Argumente. Eine Messung bisher unbekannter Clef-Latenz würde nur Zeit sparen, nicht Kosten.
429	- **Gegen Fakten aus dem Navigationsmodell (A15):** Das verlängert den kritischen Pfad deutlich.
430	- **Gegen „gar nichts tun“:**
431	  - Platz 1 auf public ist erreicht. Für das private Finale ist aber nicht Tempo entscheidend, sondern Robustheit (G-1, G-2). Und ohne Messbarkeit (O-1) bleiben weitere Tempo-Schritte blind.
432	  - Die Tempo-Schritte P-1…P-3 beseitigen Nebenwirkungen der letzten Änderung (Warteschleifen, Slot-Druck, Hedge-Doppelungen). Sie machen das System eher stabiler als riskanter.
433	
434	**Bewusst nicht verfolgt:** A3, A4, A8, A11, A14, A15, A16 (als Tempo-Instrument), A18 sowie eine Anhebung des Gesamt-Semaphors über 16.
435	
436	## 7. Anhang: wie die Zahlen entstanden sind
437	
438	**Run-Metadaten** (offizielle Zeit, Kosten, Qualität):
439	
440	    curl -H "x-api-key: $(atira token)" -A rfq-analysis https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/v1/runs/<run_id>
441	
442	**Modell-Calls:**
443	
444	    curl ... /v1/runs/<run_id>/llm-calls?limit=2000
445	
446	- Klassifikation: Navigation, wenn `input_tokens + cache_read_tokens ≥ 3300`.
447	- Sättigung: Zeitintegral über gleichzeitig offene Calls.
448	- Hedge-Paare: gleiche Prompt-Länge, zweiter Start 9–45 s nach dem ersten, vor dessen Ende.
449	
450	**Logs:**
451	
452	    curl ... /v1/runs/<run_id>/logs.jsonl
453	
454	- stdout-Zeilen als JSON parsen.
455	- Missionsende über `mission_status`, Evidenzende über `evidence_done`, Abgabe über `submit_phase_done` bzw. Actions mit `mission` = `submit@…`.
456	
457	Diese Auswertungen sollen künftig reproduzierbar über `dev/eval/bench.py` laufen (Roadmap O-2).
